lesson.title: TH → D Discrimination
lesson.subtitle: brother, mother, father, thing — separate the twins from the lookalikes

hook.title: Two Bridges at Once
hook.content: Mother is moeder and father is vader: the th→d bridge and the f→v bridge meet in the same family. Brother is broer, sister is zus. The family vocabulary is a small museum of the correspondences.

pattern.title: One family, three rules
pattern.content: Moeder shows th→d; vader shows both th→d and f→v; broer shows th→d with a vowel change. Zus is the odd one out, which is useful: not every word is a twin, and the course will never pretend otherwise.
pattern.trap_note: Do not force 'sister' into a sound rule. Zus is simply the Dutch word; learn it as an anchor and move on.

exercises.prompt: Match each English meaning with its Dutch twin (TH → D Discrimination):
exercises.target_answer: de broer, de moeder, de vader, het ding, ander, de zus
exercises.meaning: brother, mother, father, thing, other, sister
exercises.explanation: These are the anchors of "TH → D Discrimination": read each Dutch form through the pattern, not as a new word.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence says: “My mother is here.”?
exercises.explanation: “Mijn moeder is hier.” is the Dutch form; the other readings bend the pattern of “TH → D Discrimination”.

cues: The pattern: One family, three rules
It means: My father is there.
exercises.explanation: “Mijn vader is daar.” puts the thought together the Dutch way — One family, three rules.

diagnosis.slip: an English-shaped word order slipped in
diagnosis.cue: Do not force 'sister' into a sound rule. Zus is simply the Dutch word; learn it as an anchor and move on.

exercises.prompt: Which English sentence is built the Dutch way?
exercises.explanation: “Drie boeken zijn hier.” is word-for-word “Three books are here.”. The odd English is the lesson — never a model to produce. Pattern: One family, three rules.

exercises.prompt: Listen and write the whole sentence.
cues: It means: The other book is good.
exercises.explanation: “Het andere boek is goed.” reuses only material taught in “TH → D Discrimination” — One family, three rules.
exercises.affirmation: You heard “Het andere boek is goed.” — a sentence built from the lesson's own Dutch, practising One family, three rules.

twist.prompt: One more, no safety net — say: “My brother and my sister are here.”
twist.target_answer: Mijn broer en mijn zus zijn hier.
twist.explanation: Two subjects take zijn, the plural of the same being-verb.

summary.outcome: Separate real th/f twins from words that merely look similar.
summary.takeaway: A rule is strongest when you also know its exceptions.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Up next on De Brug: The F → V & S → Z Bridges.

broer.etymology_derivation: English brother and Dutch broer are cognate; Dutch shortened the word.

moeder.etymology_derivation: English mother and Dutch moeder are the same word.

vader.etymology_derivation: English father and Dutch vader are the same word with two regular correspondences.

ding.etymology_derivation: English thing and Dutch ding are the same word.

ander.etymology_derivation: English other and Dutch ander are the same word; th hardened to d.

zus.etymology_derivation: A short form of zuster; English sis is a playful cousin.

sch_sh.name: The SCH Bridge
sch_sh.phonetic_rule: English /ʃ/ (sh) corresponds to Dutch /sx/ (sch): ship → schip, shoe → schoen, sheep → schaap.
sch_sh.historical_linguistics: West Germanic *sk stayed a sk-like cluster in Dutch, spelled sch, while English palatalised it to sh.
sch_sh.philological_note: Dutch sch is not English sh; the ch is a voiceless velar fricative. School is a Latin loan shared by both languages.

th_d.name: The TH → D Bridge
th_d.phonetic_rule: English th corresponds to Dutch d: brother → broeder, three → drie, think → denken, thank → danken.
th_d.historical_linguistics: The Germanic dental fricative hardened to a stop in Dutch and German; English kept the fricative.
th_d.philological_note: Weather/weer is cognate but Dutch lost the d, so it is not a th↔d example. Loans such as theater keep t.

f_v.name: The F → V Bridge
f_v.phonetic_rule: English f often corresponds to Dutch v: father → vader, foot → voet, fish → vis.
f_v.historical_linguistics: Dutch voiced West Germanic f to v in many positions; English kept the voiceless consonant.
f_v.philological_note: Northern Dutch often devoices v to [f], especially in vr-/vl- clusters and word-finally; the spelling keeps the historical v.

s_z.name: The S → Z Bridge
s_z.phonetic_rule: English s often corresponds to Dutch z: sun → zon, sea → zee, salt → zout.
s_z.historical_linguistics: Dutch voiced West Germanic s before vowels; English kept s.
s_z.philological_note: Clusters sn/sm/sl keep s (sneeuw, smal, slapen); loans such as school and straat also keep s.

gh_ch.name: The GH → CH Bridge
gh_ch.phonetic_rule: English gh corresponds to Dutch ch: night → nacht, light → licht, right → recht, eight → acht.
gh_ch.historical_linguistics: English gh and Dutch ch descend from a shared velar fricative; English vocalised or lost it, Dutch kept it.
gh_ch.philological_note: Dutch g is the voiced partner of ch. The two are different sounds, not spelling variants.

vowel_ij.name: The IJ Bridge
vowel_ij.phonetic_rule: Dutch ij is /ɛi/ and often answers to English i/y: ice → ijs, wine → wijn, five → vijf.
vowel_ij.historical_linguistics: The digraph ij spells a Dutch diphthong; English orthography kept a different vowel from the same Germanic stock.
vowel_ij.philological_note: IJ is two letters but one sound. It is not English /aɪ/.

vowel_ui.name: The UI Bridge
vowel_ui.phonetic_rule: Dutch ui is /œy/ and often answers to English ou/ow: house → huis, mouse → muis, out → uit.
vowel_ui.historical_linguistics: Dutch ui spells a front rounded diphthong with no close English equivalent; the English spelling twin is a memory hook.
vowel_ui.philological_note: Do not pronounce ui as two English beats; it is one gliding vowel.

vowel_oe.name: The OE Bridge
vowel_oe.phonetic_rule: Dutch oe is /u/ and often answers to English oo/u in spelling: book → boek, foot → voet, good → goed.
vowel_oe.historical_linguistics: The Dutch digraph oe spells a long /u/; English oo spells several different vowels, so this is a spelling/cognacy bridge.
vowel_oe.philological_note: Dutch oe is /u/, not the /ʊ/ of English book. Read the Dutch spelling and use the Dutch sound.

g_y.name: The G / Y Bridge
g_y.phonetic_rule: English g and some y words correspond to voiced Dutch g: gold → goud, good → goed, yellow → geel.
g_y.historical_linguistics: Dutch kept a velar fricative where English kept a stop or palatalised to y. English year/jaar is y↔j, not y↔g.
g_y.philological_note: Dutch g is a fricative, never the English stop in 'good'.
